papers.title_in_file: Noise-Resilient Single-Pixel Compressive Sensing with Single Photon Counting
papers.version_note: Research Square preprint, posted October 10th, 2023 (DOI 10.21203/rs.3.rs-3349937/v1). Page 1 states that a version was published at Communications Physics on March 29th, 2024. The supplementary files (Figures S10 and S11, Tables S1 and S2) are a separate file and are not in this PDF.

figures.shows: Research Square banner image (logo) and its preprint disclaimer line at the top of the cover page; it carries no data.

Experimental layout: MLL, WDMs and EDFAs split into probe and pump; probe goes through attenuator, 99:1 beamsplitter, DMD (Walsh patterns), SLM (MNIST digits), then a 50:50 beamsplitter to the InGaAs SPD (direct detection) and, with the pump, through the PPLN module to the Si SPD (QPMS); a time tagger records both; ASE noise is added at the 50:50 beamsplitter. Insets (a) to (e) are normalized spectra (y, normalized power in dB; x, wavelength in nm): probe near 1554 nm, pump near 1564 nm, broad ASE near 1500 to 1600 nm, wavelength-selected ASE near 1554 nm, upconverted output near 780 nm.
figures.confirmed_by: The experimental setup is sketched in Fig. 1.

figures.shows: (a) raw per-event DD photon counts (y, 0 to 150) against event index over 80 patterns (x, 0 to 800); (b) raw per-event QPMS photon counts (y, 0 to 400) over 80 patterns (x, 0 to 2000); (c) mean QPMS photon counts per pattern (y, 0 to 200) against pattern index (x, 0 to 300); (d) fully connected network diagram with 300 input values, 7 layers in total, and 10 outputs labeled 0 to 9.
figures.confirmed_by: Fig. 2(b) shows their average for each of the 300 patterns uploaded onto the DMD, which extract 300 features from each digit image.

figures.shows: Four normalized confusion matrices (real label on y, predicted label on x, digits 0 to 9, color scale 0 to 1, cell values printed). (a) DD, 600 us per mask, 398.6 average photons, 82.8% accuracy; (b) DD, 800 us, 551.2 photons, 90%; (c) DD, 800 us, 391.5 photons, probe about 8.5 nW, 80.4%; (d) QPMS, 200 us, 485.8 photons, 98%. DD matrices show off-diagonal mass mainly between digits 5 and 6 and between 6 and 8 and between 3 and 8; QPMS (d) is near-diagonal, lowest diagonal cell 0.92.
figures.confirmed_by: As an example, Fig. 3 shows the confusion matrices for both DD and QPMS under different integration times and different probe powers.

figures.shows: Dark (background) photon counts (y, 0 to 30) against integration time on the SPDs (x, 0 to 100 us). Red triangles (direct detection, InGaAs SPD) rise from about 4 at about 15 us to about 29 at 100 us along a fitted line. Green diamonds (QPMS detection, Si SPD) rise from under 1 at about 3 us to about 8 at about 40 us along a lower fitted line. The caption calls both fits quadratic; they look close to linear.
figures.confirmed_by: To check this, Fig. 4 plots the measured dark counts of the two detection channels.

figures.shows: Classification accuracy (y, 20 to 100 %) against average photon counts (x, 0 to 2000). Five series: QPMS with 300, 100 and 40 masks, and DD with 300 and 100 masks. DD (300 masks) rises from about 42 at about 60 photons to about 90 at about 550; DD (100 masks) from about 26 to about 82. QPMS (300 masks) starts at about 97 near 120 photons; QPMS (100 masks) at about 93; QPMS (40 masks) at about 91, dips to about 88 near 250, and all three QPMS series reach about 99 by about 1000 photons and stay there to about 2000.
figures.confirmed_by: Figure 5 summarizes the classiﬁcation accuracy as a function of the average detected photon number per DMD mask, for both detection channels and different number of DMD masks used.

figures.shows: Classification accuracy (y, 20 to 100 %) against SNR of the ASE noise (x, -30 to 10 dB). QPMS with 300 masks is about 94 at -27 dB and about 98 or higher from about -23 dB to 3 dB; QPMS with 100 masks is about 88 at -27 dB, about 97 at about -23 dB, and about 98 or higher from -20 dB. DD has two points only: 300 masks about 22 at 0 dB and about 52 at 3 dB; 100 masks about 21 at 0 dB and about 39 at 3 dB.
figures.confirmed_by: The results are shown in Fig. 6.

figures.shows: Two normalized confusion matrices for QPMS detection (real label on y, predicted on x, digits 0 to 9, color scale 0 to 1, cell values printed). (a) trained at SNR 0 dB and tested with no noise; diagonal cells 0.92 to 1. (b) trained at SNR -10 dB and tested at SNR -17 dB; diagonal cells 0.92 to 1, with 0.08 of digit 3 predicted as 9. The figure is cited in the text as the supplementary figure 7.
figures.confirmed_by: The results are shown in the supplementary ﬁgure 7, with (a) for the training at 0 dB SNR and testing without noise and (b) for the training at -10 dB SNR and testing at -17 dB.

papers.what_it_is: An experimental study of how dark counts and in-band noise degrade single-pixel compressive-sensing classification of MNIST digits by a neural network, comparing a direct-detection InGaAs single-photon detector with quantum parametric mode sorting (QPMS) upconversion detection.

assertions.value: The authors report 94% classification accuracy of MNIST digits in the presence of in-band noise 500 times stronger than the received signal.
quotes: We achieve 94% classiﬁcation accuracy in the presence of 500 times stronger in-band noise than the signal received.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one experiment.
assertions.reader_inference: The 94% is for QPMS with 300 masks at an SNR of -27 dB (Section Results, p.8). The experiment uses 1000 digits with a 25% test share and no repeated runs or error bars are reported.

assertions.value: The authors state that QPMS, using broadband pump pulses with a spectral width comparable to the phasematching bandwidth of the frequency converter, selectively converts single photons in a custom spatiotemporal mode where the returning signal photons are expected, so that background photons in other modes are rejected efficiently even when they overlap the probe in space and time.
quotes: By using broadband pump pulses with a spectral width comparable to the phasematching bandwidth of the frequency converter
QPMS is able to selectively convert single photons in a custom spatiotemporal mode39, where the returning signal photons are expected.
background photons in other modes will be rejected efﬁciently, even when they are spatial and temporal overlap with the probe.
assertions.certainty_reason: A mechanism the paper attributes to earlier work (reference 39), not established here.

assertions.value: The authors use a total of 1000 MNIST handwritten digits as targets, 75% for training and 25% for testing, each sampled by 40, 100 or 300 Walsh 2D patterns, which they give as compression ratios of 0.07%, 0.17% and 0.52%.
quotes: we use a total of 1000 MNIST handwritten digits as our targets, with 75% for training and 25% for testing, each sampled by 40, 100, or 300 Walsh 2D patterns, corresponding to a compression ratio of 0.07%, 0.17%, or 0.52%, respectively.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own experimental setup.
assertions.reader_inference: A 25% share of 1000 digits is 250 test digits; the confusion-matrix cells in multiples of 0.04 (Figure 3, p.5) fit 25 test digits per class. Each reported accuracy therefore rests on about 250 test samples.

assertions.value: The authors vary the photon-counting integration time between 15 µs and 100 µs for direct detection, with average counts per mask of 59.5 to 551.2 photons, and between 3 µs and 40 µs for QPMS, with average counts per mask of 119.7 to 1990.6 photons.
quotes: we vary the photon counting integration time between 15 µs and 100 µs for the direct detection (DD) system with counts on average per mask 59.5 to 551.2 photons
while varying the photon counting integration time between 3 µs and 40 µs for the QPMS system with average counts per mask as 119.7 to 1990.6 photons.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own experimental setup and range.

assertions.value: The authors report that for direct detection the classification accuracy drops significantly when the mean photon numbers fall below 300.
quotes: Our results ﬁnd that for DD, the accuracy drops signiﬁcantly when the mean photon numbers fall below 300.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors report that adding in-band noise at 50% and 100% of the probe power lowers direct-detection accuracy to around 51.6% and 22% from 80.2%.
quotes: When adding in-band noise at a 50% and 100% level as the probe power, the accuracy drops to around 51.6% and 22% from 80.2% for DD.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.
assertions.reader_inference: The Introduction gives the no-noise baseline as 80.2%, while the Results (p.7) give 80.4% for the same Figure 3(c) condition. The paper does not reconcile the two.

assertions.value: The authors report that with 500 times more background photons than signal, the QPMS classification accuracy drops only from about 99% to 94%.
quotes: Even when there are 500 times more background photons than the signal, the classiﬁcation accuracy drops only from about 99% to 94%.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors report that sampling targets with 100 Walsh 2D patterns instead of 300 lowers the direct-detection accuracy by about 10%, while no obvious change happens to QPMS detection in the data without ASE noise.
quotes: We also try to sample targets with 100 Walsh 2D patterns for a higher compression ratio.
The classiﬁcation accuracy of DD decreases for ∼10% compared with sample targets with 300 Walsh 2D patterns
but no obvious change happens to QPMS detection
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors report that for the data with ASE noise, no notable change happens to QPMS detection when the SNR level is larger than -20dB, while a change of about 30% happens to direct detection at an SNR level of 3dB, in the comparison of 100 against 300 Walsh 2D patterns.
quotes: We also try to sample targets with 100 Walsh 2D patterns for a higher compression ratio.
compared with sample targets with 300 Walsh 2D patterns
no notable change happens to QPMS detection when the SNR level is larger than -20dB, while ∼30% happens to the DD when the SNR level is 3dB.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study, stated in the Introduction in condensed form.
assertions.reader_inference: The sentence does not say what quantity changes by about 30%. Figure 6 (p.7) shows DD accuracy about 52% against about 39% at 3 dB for 300 against 100 masks, which is a gap of roughly 13 points, not 30.

assertions.value: The authors describe a femtosecond mode-locked laser at a repetition rate of 50 MHz, split into a 6 ps probe pulse centered at 1554.3 nm and a 6 ps pump pulse centered at 1564.3 nm.
quotes: operating at a repetition rate of 50 MHz.
inset (a) represents the spectrum of 6 ps probe pulse centered at 1554.3 nm, while inset (b) represents the 6 ps pump pulse centered at 1564.3 nm.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own experimental setup.

assertions.value: The authors encode MNIST digit images on the SLM as binary phase patterns, each pixel either 0 or 3π/8, and resize the 28×28 images to 240×240 to match the probe beam diameter.
quotes: Each pixel in the phase patterns is expressed as a binary phase value of either 0 or 3π/8.
To ensure the MNIST 28×28 digit images align with the probe beam diameter on our SLM, we resize them to 240×240 images.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own experimental setup.

assertions.value: The authors set the quantum efficiency of the gated InGaAs single-photon detector to 20%, with a 1 ns effective gate width, giving a total detection efficiency of 4.2% for the direct-detection channel after fiber connector and filter losses.
quotes: the quantum efﬁciency of the gated (1 ns effective gate width) InGaAs-SPD is set to be 20%, with losses in ﬁber connectors and ﬁlters, giving a total detection efﬁciency of 4.2% for the DD channel.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own experimental setup.

assertions.value: The authors give the Si single-photon detector a quantum efficiency of 66% and the QPMS channel a total detection efficiency of 12.0% after fiber connector and filter losses.
quotes: the Si-SPD has a quantum efﬁciency of 66%.
the total detection efﬁciency for the QPMS channel is 12.0%.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own experimental setup.

assertions.value: The authors report that the upconverted QPMS output operates at a wavelength of 779.59 nm and is detected by a silicon single-photon detector.
quotes: The resulting output, operating at a wavelength of 779.59 nm, is then detected using a silicon SPD (Si-SPD, Excelitas).
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own experimental setup.

assertions.value: The authors generate in-band ASE noise with an EDFA and pass it through a 1554.1 nm WDM, which aligns the noise within the same wavelength range as the probe.
quotes: The ASE noise is then combined with the probe by passing it through a 1554.1 nm WDM, which aligns the noise within the same wavelength range as the probe.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own experimental setup.

assertions.value: The authors acquire 300 photon counts for 300 Walsh 2D patterns for each handwritten digit and use them as 300 features, the inputs to the deep neural network.
quotes: For each handwritten digit, 300 photon counts for 300 Walsh 2D patterns are acquired as shown in Fig. 2(a, b).
which extract 300 features from each digit image.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own experimental setup.

assertions.value: The authors average the QPMS photon counts for each DMD pattern over 20 of 25 events, dropping the first three and last two events while the system settles during the pattern transition, for an effective integration time of 0.8 millisecond in the example.
quotes: Example mean photon counts of QPMS for each DMD pattern by averaging over 20 of the 25 events, where the ﬁrst three and last two events are dropped as the systems settles during the pattern transition. The effective integration time of photon counting is thus 0.8 millisecond in this case.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own data-processing setup.
assertions.reader_inference: The Model text (p.4) calls Fig. 2(a) the QPMS raw counts and Fig. 2(b) their average, while the caption labels (a) as DD raw, (b) as QPMS raw and (c) as the QPMS mean. The text and caption panel labels disagree.

assertions.value: The authors average the direct-detection photon counts for each DMD pattern over 8 of 10 events, dropping the first and last events while the system settles during the pattern transition, with each event counting photons for 100 µs.
quotes: Mean photon counts of DD for each DMD pattern by averaging over 8 of the 10 events, where the ﬁrst and last events are dropped as the systems settles during the pattern transition.
where each event counts photons for 100 µs, and there are 10 events for each DMD pattern
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own data-processing setup.

assertions.value: The authors add two white patterns to the end of the existing 300 pattern sequence to distinguish each target uploaded onto the SLM.
quotes: In the experiment, two white patterns
are added to the end of the existing 300 pattern sequence, to serve the purpose of distinguishing each target uploaded onto the SLM.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own experimental setup.

assertions.value: The authors use a deep neural network with a total of 7 layers: the input layer, five hidden layers and the output layer, with ReLU activation functions on the hidden layers and a log-softmax function between the second last layer and the last layer.
quotes: The DNN consists of a total of 7 layers including the input layer, ﬁve hidden layers, and the output layer.
ReLU activation functions are applied to the hidden layers, while a log-softmax function is used between the second last layer and the last layer.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own model setup.
assertions.reader_inference: The text gives no layer widths, optimizer, learning rate or loss; only the epoch counts appear in the figure captions.

assertions.value: The authors use 100 different MNIST images for each digit, for 10 digits a total of 1000 samples, each containing 300 mean photon counts, with 75% of the samples as training data and 25% as testing.
quotes: there are 100 different images for each digit from the MNIST dataset. For 10 digits, the amounts to a total of 1000 samples, each containing 300 mean photon counts.
For classiﬁcation, we allocate 75% of the samples as the training data and 25% as testing.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own dataset setup.

assertions.value: The authors state that the changing pattern time on the DMD is about 100 µs and that the photon-counting events during that time are disregarded when the data are processed.
quotes: The changing pattern time on the DMD is ∼100 µs. When we process the data from the experiment setup, disregard these photon-counting events during the changing pattern time on the DMD.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own data-processing setup.

assertions.value: The authors use 300 training epochs for direct detection and 200 training epochs for QPMS detection in the confusion-matrix results.
quotes: using 300 training epochs for DD and 200 training epochs for QPMS detection.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own training setup.
assertions.reader_inference: DD and QPMS use different epoch counts, so the accuracy comparison between them is not at a matched training budget.

assertions.value: The authors report that with a 600 µs integration time per mask on the InGaAs SPD and a probe power of about 14 nW, the average photon count per mask is 398.6, giving an 82.8% classification accuracy.
quotes: when the integration time per mask is 600 µs for the InGaAs SPD and the probe power is ∼14 nW, the average photon counts per mask is 398.6, which gives an 82.8% classiﬁcation accuracy.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors report that raising the integration time to 800 µs at the same probe power gives an average of 551.2 photons per mask and a classification accuracy that improves to 90%.
quotes: it to 800 µs but keeping the probe power, the average photon count per mask becomes 551.2, and the classiﬁcation accuracy improves to 90%.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors report that with the same 800 µs integration time and the probe power reduced to about 8.5 nW, the average photon count per mask is 391.5 and the classification accuracy drops to 80.4%.
quotes: with the same 800 µs integration time but reducing the probe power to ∼8.5 nW, the average photon counts per mask is 391.5, and the classiﬁcation accuracy drops to 80.4%, as shown in Fig. 3(c).
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors report that at a probe power of about 4 nW with the same 800 µs integration time, the average photon count is 299.7 and the classification accuracy is only 31.6%.
quotes: as the probe power drops down to ∼4 nW (while keeping the same 800 µs integration time), the average photon counts is 299.7, for which the classiﬁcation accuracy is only 31.6%.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors state that these results show the accuracy depends on the photon counts, whose fluctuations are governed by shot noise, so that with higher photon counts the measurement uncertainty is reduced and the recognition accuracy is higher.
quotes: These results highlight the accuracy dependency on the photon counts, whose ﬂuctuations are governed by shot noise.
with higher photon counts, the measurement uncertainty is reduced, so that the recognition accuracy is higher.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author interpretation; no test separating shot noise from dark counts is reported.
assertions.reader_inference: The same section later attributes the DD shortfall mainly to dark counts, so shot noise and dark counts are both offered as causes.

assertions.value: The authors report that with a QPMS integration time of 200 µs and a probe power of about 14 nW, the average photon count per DMD mask is 485.8 and the classification accuracy is 98%.
quotes: With an integration time of 200 µs and probe power of ∼14 nW, the average photon count per DMD mask is 485.8.
The classiﬁcation accuracy in this case is 98%, which is signiﬁcantly higher than the DD case with similar or even higher photon counts.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors state that the higher photon counts for QPMS despite a shorter integration time result from a higher total detection efficiency of 12.0% versus 4.2% for the direct-detection channel.
quotes: The higher photon counts despite a shorter integration time is a result of a higher total detection efﬁciency for QPMS 12.0% versus 4.2% for the DD channel.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author explanation of a measured difference.

assertions.value: The authors state that the much better performance of QPMS over direct detection is mainly attributed to its much lower dark counts.
quotes: The much better performance in QPMS over DD as seen in Fig. 3 is mainly attributed to its much lower dark counts.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author attribution; no ablation separates dark counts from the efficiency difference.
assertions.reader_inference: The two channels differ in detector type, efficiency, dark counts and saturation level together, and the paper offers efficiency as a second cause (p.7), so no single factor is isolated.

assertions.value: The authors report measured dark-count rates of about 0.29 per 10 microsecond integration time for direct detection and about 0.21 per 10 µs for QPMS.
quotes: 0.29 per 10 microsecond integration time for DD, and about 0.21 per 10 µs for QPMS.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.
assertions.reader_inference: The stated unit looks wrong by a factor of 10. Figure 4 shows about 29 dark counts at 100 µs for DD, which is about 0.29 per µs, and the text's own 234 per 800 µs, 11.8 per 40 µs (DD) and 8.5 per 40 µs (QPMS) all fit a rate per µs, not per 10 µs. The sentence is likely a typo for per µs.

assertions.value: The authors report that the dark count translates to 234 per 800 µs integration time for the direct-detection channel in Figure 3(b), about half of the average photon count, and to only 40 per 200 µs for the QPMS channel in Figure 3(d), about 8.2% of the average count.
quotes: They translate to 234 per 800 µs integration time for the DD channel in Fig. 3(b), which is about half of the average photon count.
the dark count is only 40 per 200 µs integration time for the QPMS channel in Fig. 3(d), about 8.2% of the average count.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.
assertions.reader_inference: 40 of 485.8 is 8.2%, and 234 of 551.2 is about 42%, so the paper's figures are consistent with each other.

assertions.value: The authors report that the InGaAs SPD dark count can be reduced to only 0.01 per 10 microsecond by setting the quantum efficiency to 15%, but that the saturation counts are then lowered by more than a half, reducing the dynamic range of detected signal photons.
quotes: in our experiment, the dark count for the InGaAs SPD can be reduced to only 0.01 per 10 microsecond by setting quantum efﬁciency to 15%. However, the saturation counts will be lowered by more than a half, so that the dynamic range of detected signal photons is reduced.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.
assertions.reader_inference: The 0.01 per 10 microsecond carries the same unit ambiguity as the 0.29 per 10 microsecond figure.

assertions.value: The authors state that the Si-SPD has orders of magnitude lower dark counts, at least 10 times higher saturation counts and several times higher efficiency than the InGaAs SPD.
quotes: In comparison, Si-SPD has a much better performance in this perspective, with orders of magnitude lower dark counts, at least 10 times higher saturation counts, and several times higher efﬁciency.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim given without a table of measured values in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors report that for QPMS at an average photon number of 119.7 per mask the accuracy is 97.2% with 300 masks and 93.2% with 100 masks, and that at higher counts it saturates to 99.2% for both cases when the average photon count increases to around 500.
quotes: when the average photon number is 119.7 per mask, the accuracy is 97.2% with 300 masks and 93.2% with 100 masks.
the accuracy ﬂuctuates a bit but quickly saturates to 99.2% for both cases, when the average photon count increases to around 500.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors report that for direct detection at 59.5 average photon count the accuracy is 42.4% with 300 masks and only 26.4% with 100 masks, and that at an average count of 550 it increases to around 90% and 82.8% respectively.
quotes: with 59.5 average photon count, it is 42.4% with 300 masks and only 26.4% with 100 masks.
As the average count increases to 550, the accuracy increases to around 90% and 82.8%, respectively, for the two mask numbers
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors state that, due to the InGaAs-SPD saturation, the average photon count cannot be further increased for the direct-detection channel.
quotes: Due to the InGaAs-SPD saturation, the average photon count cannot be further increased for the DD channel.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state a limit of their own measurement: direct detection could not be tested above about 551 photons per mask.
assertions.reader_inference: The DD curves in Figure 5 stop near 551 photons, so the comparison above that count has no DD data.

assertions.value: The authors state that the much better performance of QPMS over direct detection is due to a much higher total detection efficiency (12.0% vs 4.2%) and a lower dark count, so that the percentage of true signal photons in the total photon counts is much higher.
quotes: to a much higher total detection efﬁciency (12.0% vs 4.2%) and a lower dark count, so that the percentage of true signal
assertions.certainty_reason: An author attribution of a measured difference.

assertions.value: The authors state that, as shown in Fig. 5, when the number of masks is decreased for DD and QPMS, the classification accuracy of QPMS drops less than that of DD.
quotes: as we decrease masks for DD and QPMS, the classiﬁcation accuracy of QPMS drops less than DD.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors state that Figures 3 to 5 present the results without external background noise, where the noise photon counts come from within the detection systems, including APD dark counts and Raman scattering noises in the QPMS module.
quotes: Figures 3-5 present the results without external background noise, where the noise photon counts are from within the detection systems, including APD dark counts and Raman scattering noises in the QPMS module.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the scope of its own results in Figures 3 to 5.

assertions.value: The authors define the signal to noise ratio as 10 log10 [(Noff − Ndark)/(Ntot − Noff)], where Noff is the photon count without ASE, Ndark is the same count with the probe shut off, and Ntot is the same count with the added ASE noise.
quotes: Its strength relative to the signal, i.e., the signal to noise ratio (SNR), is deﬁned as 10 log10 [(Noff − Ndark)/(Ntot − Noff)].
Ndarkis the same photon counts but with the probe shut off. Ntot is the same photon counts but with the added ASE noise.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines its own SNR measure where it is first used.
assertions.reader_inference: Because Noff and Ntot come from one pattern, SNR is a per-measurement ratio, not an average over the digit set.

assertions.value: The authors take Noff as the photon counts registered by the InGaAs SPD with the first image of digit 1 from the MNIST dataset on the SLM and the 31st Walsh 2D pattern on the DMD, which gives the highest photon counts over all combinations used in the experiment.
quotes: Here Noff is the photon counts without ASE, as registered by the InGaAs SPD with the ﬁrst image of digit 1 from MNIST dataset on SLM and set the 31st Walsh 2D pattern we generated on DMD, which gives the highest photon counts over all combinations used in this experiment.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states how its own SNR reference level is measured.
assertions.reader_inference: SNR is referenced to the brightest single pattern, so the stated SNR overstates the signal relative to the average pattern; the paper does not say by how much.

assertions.value: The authors set the effective dwell time of each Walsh 2D pattern on the DMD to 800 µs for the ASE-noise baseline, with an integration time of 100 µs on the InGaAs SPD and always 40 µs on the Si SPD.
quotes: In this particular case, the effective dwell time of each Walsh 2D pattern on the DMD is set to 800 µs. The integration time on InGaAs SPD is 100 µs, while the integration time on Si SPD is always 40 µs.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own experimental setup.
assertions.reader_inference: Figure 3 captions call 800 µs the integration time per mask for DD, while this passage gives 100 µs per event on the InGaAs SPD; the 800 µs appears to be the sum of the 8 retained 100 µs events (Figure 2 caption).

assertions.value: The authors report that the direct-detection accuracy is 80.4% with 300 masks after 300 epochs of training at a probe power of about 8.5 nW and SPD dark counts of about 234, and that it drops to 41.2% at a probe power of about 6 nW and to 31.6% at about 4 nW.
quotes: the classiﬁcation accuracy for DD is 80.4% with 300 masks after 300 epochs of training as shown in Fig. 3(c) with the probe power ∼8.5 nW and the SPD dark counts ∼234.
the classiﬁcation accuracy drops to 41.2% with the probe power ∼6 nW, and to 31.6% with the probe power ∼4 nW.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors state that for the Si SPD, with much less dark counts and a much higher saturation level, the probe power can be attenuated to around 6 nW so that the SNR can be as low as -27 dB for QPMS.
quotes: we are able to attenuate the prob power to around ∼6 nW so that the SNR
can be as low as -27 dB for QPMS.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors report that with the probe power about 8.5 nW and ASE power set equal to the probe (SNR of 0 dB), the direct-detection photon counts for all patterns vary between 67 and 115 and the classification accuracy is only 22.0% after 300 training epochs with 300 masks.
quotes: the probe power after the FC1 is set to be about 8.5 nW.
